who is being left behind in lapland and.text:
**Who is left behind in Lapland:**
Patients entering via public health centres with basic education, living far from the hospital (157 km), and facing navigation barriers wait up to **222.4 days** from symptoms to treatment (~2.1 patients/year; 141.8 extra days vs the best-placed patient). The public entry route accounts for 67.3 days of delay, and travel distance adds 37.8 days. Only 20.4% of Lapland patients begin treatment within 42 days of referral.

**Recommended actions:**
- **Step Zero:** Deploy the minimum dataset to record symptom, referral, and treatment dates [ROADMAP p.58, p.59].
- **Standardised fast-track pathway:** Saves an estimated 16.4 days overall [ROADMAP p.52, p.56].
- **Targeted low-effort wins:** Symptom-awareness campaigns [ROADMAP p.33] and travel coordination support [ROADMAP p.63].

*Note: Pathway metrics are modelled estimates; entry-route differences reflect lymphoma data applied to lung cancer.*

why does patient b wait so much longer t.text:
Patient B faces an estimated total delay of 225.5 days compared to 94.1 days for Patient A—a gap of **131.4 days** (with 69.5% occurring before referral).

The modelled factors driving Patient B's extra wait are:
- **Entry route (+72.5 days):** Relying on public primary care rather than occupational health [ROADMAP p.11, p.51–52].
- **Travel distance (+43.6 days):** Living 180 km from the central hospital vs. 8 km [ROADMAP p.13].
- **Education & health literacy (+15.6 days):** Slower symptom recognition and navigation [STRATEGY p.19, ROADMAP p.10].
- **Navigation barriers (+13.2 days):** Living alone or aged 75+ without care coordination [STRATEGY p.17, ROADMAP p.32].
- **County capacity difference:** -13.5 days.

*Note: Modelled estimates; entry-route impact assumes lymphoma pathway dynamics applied to lung cancer.*

what does the national roadmap say about.text:
The national roadmap establishes standardised referral criteria under **Action 2.5.2** [ROADMAP p.52] and **Action 3.1.2** [ROADMAP p.56], adopting Nordic fast-track models (such as Danish *Kræftpakkeforløb* and Swedish *SVF*) to define symptom-based criteria and direct diagnostic pathways.

For Lapland, implementing a standardised fast-track pathway is modelled to achieve:
- **16.4 days saved** on average (evidence range: 6.8–31.1 days), cutting total pathway time from 165.2 to 148.8 days.
- Patients treated within the 42-day target rising from 21.5% to 38.6%.
- Equity gap narrowing from 141.8 to 131.2 days.

*Note on confidence:* These pathway figures are modelled estimates based on preliminary Finnish phase data and Nordic implementation evidence (confidence: medium); decision support only.

which regions lose the most time and is.text:
The slowest modelled pathway times occur in **North Karelia** (176.2 days), **North Ostrobothnia** (174.0 days), and **Central Finland** (173.6 days). 

The data indicates this is primarily an **equity and geography problem**, not simple hospital capacity:

* **Disparities dominate capacity:** The intra-county equity gap ranges from 113.3 to **141.8 days** (widest in Lapland), far exceeding the 41.3-day variance across county averages.
* **Geography drives delays:** In Lapland, specialist waits are 6.4 days faster than national average, but distance alone adds 17.2 days. Entry route and navigation hurdles drive the remaining divide [ROADMAP p.12–13].
* Addressing this requires standardized care chains and decentralized pathways [ROADMAP p.52, 56].

*(Note: Regional estimates are modelled; national pathway times are preliminary, and entry-route effects adapt Finnish lymphoma data.)*
